items.body:
In 'The Rhythm of Design', Zurich-based fine arts duo Michael Meier & Christoph Franz explore urban displacement and its impact on the local music scene.

"Focusing on six venues that have disappeared or are under threat, the artists collected materials on site - wood, metal, and other architectural elements and, with the support of professional instrument builders, transformed them into six musical instruments. Six artists and groups connected to these spaces, namely Kalabrese, Tobibi Ferrari-Bienz, Rafal Skoczek, Lucien Badoux & Jeremy Sauter, Nicola Kazimir, and Dualism each composed a piece for them, forming the basis for site-specific performances in September 2025. Rather than performing as an ensemble, the works ranging from experimental funk and punk to kraut, noise, and drone unfolded simultaneously in spatial fragments at the original locations. Only through movement and listening across the city did the composition emerge as a whole. The work was realized in collaboration with the City of Zurich, Art in Public Space (KiöR). Eight months after the original performances took place, the pieces are released via Switzerland-based publishing platform Präsens Editionen."

Sandy B’s classic ‘90s SA kwaito templates are lent a subtly trippy, brooding sidespin by Belgian DJ, producer and compiler soFa Elsewhere, sealed with artwork by Cape Town’s Darren Christian.

‘Forward in Reverse (Pt. 1)’ is a crafty effort at replicating and adapting a sound perhaps best recognised for the likes of Sandy B’s ‘AmaJovi Jovi’ heater of ’94, as reissued to cult acclaim in 2017 by Awesome Tapes From Africa. One of only a handful of efforts at reviving the sound that we can recall, the seven tracks nail an ace balance of the OG ‘90s sound - a sort of ruggedly hypnotic, slower take on deep house - with more psychedelic detailing and added political impetus in Sandy’s pointed lyrics, which sometimes slip into english from his native KwaZulu-Natal region’s Zulu tongue. The difference can be attributed to Sandy B’s lived experience of the past 30 years since ‘AmaJovi…’ and the moodier tone of soFa Elsewhere’s input, perhaps emphasising a long latent parallel with ‘80s hip house or Belgian new beat’s pace and purpose. 

Sandy voices each cut in a mix of choral harmony, undulating sing-song and rapped spoken word, flowing effortlessly between them on opener ‘Mangamanga’, or suitably kitted with new beat-esque heave-ho and wickedly scribbly synth on ‘Siren Work’, and sunken to moodiest hunch on ‘Khuluma Kakhulu.’ His politics come to the fore in the exasperated delivery and refrain “what’s wrong with you / you selfish bastard” on the (corruption) house grind of ‘Politicians’ and taken to slowest, dankest levels in ‘Eat Promises’, or like a mardy Francis Bebey in ‘ Mo-fucka’, and the martial swag of ‘Isosha Elidakiwe (Drunk Soldier)’ could almost have emerged from the Teknokrat’s studio in ’89.

items.body:
The roots of so much modern groove-driven music are reflected in Soundway’s study of rare jazz, calypso and drum music from ‘70s Trinidad & Tobago, the Caribbean nation off the coast of Venezuela.

In that time between artists first plugging in their instruments, and computerising them, the psychedelic sheen and sonification of US & UK pop and dance musics would also rub off on modernisers in the Caribbean. Under the Trinidadian term for calypso, “kaiso” the artists showcased here would blend Afro-American and West Indian traditions with certain studio innovations from disco and psych-rock to a clear purpose: driving dances - and everything that comes with them - in their lush isles.

The results are hip-gripping, heat-seeking gems that factor Black Atlantic links for a new, independent era un-tethered from colonial influence, ranging from the deeply soul-stirring jazz hush and rumble of ‘Ogun’ by Clive Zanda, thru Abdul Malik de Coteau’s plangent lament set to air-rippling steel drums, taking in the spiritual Latin jazz of Michael Boothman’s ‘Tabu’ brimming with optimism, to the muy caliente calypso of Andre Tanker, heads-down drum vibrations of Mansa Musa, and psych-funk fusioneering of Frends on ‘Mystery Music’.

items.body:
Following records on Quiet Time and Miami's Schematic, Cairo-based producer Mostafa Onsy arrives on the mighty Drowned By Locals with a unique adaptation of 808 Mafia's iconic trap sound that pulls in influences from classic '90s Egyptian pop and mahraganat.

'Baba Fen' might come as a surprise if you've heard Onsy's previous records, like 2021's dark, trippy IDM suite 'MetaConc' and its predecessor, a nostalgia trip that took its blueprint from AFX's '90s gear. Here, the producer takes his cues from Southside, TM88 and Lex Luger's iconic Atlanta trap productions: the ratcheting hi-hats, overdriven 808 kicks and acidic trance risers that characterized American music in the wake of breakouts from Future. Honestly, it works - we've long maintained the similarities between IDM's skittering beats and trap's, and Onsy's a natural, dropping a familiar ATL snare and FL Studio synths between mahraganat hand drums and those ubiquitous pitched hi-hat runs on the scene-setting 'Zabet Ekaa3 (Intro)'.

He's joined by local vocalists Fara7 and Bleng on 'Fnan', who help assert the album's Egyptian relevance, draping their melancholy AutoTuned slurs and ad-libs around Onsy's clever fusion of half-speed local percussion and trap's signature soundset. And the two MCs are joined by gravelly-voiced rapper Sakt on the album's brilliant title track, where Onsy supplies his spookies FM-laced beats, phonk-adjacent slaps that wouldn't be out of place on one of Raider Klan's early mixtapes. Rubber-voiced Drowned By Locals regular illfeel shows up on 'Fantanyel' and goes toe-to-toe with Bleng on 'Blikii', trading blows over one of Onsy's most ominous productions. Recommended.

items.body:
Recorded straight to tape in Glasgow, poet/performer Lisa Jones and VOM's Chas Lalli's Gilchard debut is refreshingly human, a grotesque blend of ugly reality and absurdity that situates itself between Electrelane, Arab Strap, Dry Cleaning and early Factory biz.

'Chins for Lefty' might be Gilchard's first recording, but Jones and Lalli are hardly newcomers. Since the mid-'00s, Lalli has been a member of Glaswegian post-punk/noise rock trio VOM, moonlighting in Bad Aura and the art-punk outfit Dragged Up, where he first collided with Jones. A writer and poet with a background in the local spoken word/improv scene, Jones' lyrics provide the backbone for Gilchard's sound, building a surreal parallel Glasgow that Lalli meets head-on with jangling guitars, frazzled drum loops and murky synths. Even the recording process itself plays a part, lending the album a timeless quality - honestly if you assured us this was an excavated private press gem from the late '80s we'd probably believe you.

"I turn your picture to face the wall," Jones deadpans on 'Posthumous Hologram', breaking her monotone to sing a real chorus while Lalli stacks organ vamps and Vini Reilly guitars in the space beneath. And the duo decelerate their sound significantly on 'Break Up with Johnny Dogbirth', sounding as heroin-addled as The Velvet Underground as they work in slow motion, batting emotional reflections to each other over an almost inaudible drum beat.

items.body:
Italian ambient maestro Gigi Masin returns to his happy place on 'Movement', following 2020's 'Calypso' with a record that surveys a quarter century of vintage back room sounds, pulling from kosmische, new age, early techno, glitch and balearic house. 

For the last few years, Masin has been busy with a litany of collaborations, working with Jonny Nash and Young Marco as Gaussian Curve, with dub techno OG Rod Modell on 2023's 'Red Hair Girl at Lighthouse Beach and with jazz pianist Greg Foat on a ruck of soundtrack-y downtempo material. In fact it's been years since his last solo release; the Apollo-released 'Calypso' came out six years ago and 'Movement' appears to pick up where it left off. The waterlogged, sun-bleached concept is all but gone, but the sounds, cherry-picked from across the downtempo spectrum, are very much in keeping. 

Opener 'Bed on Mars' is classic Masin and should appeal to fans of his cult 1986 breakout 'Wind', the long-overlooked album that featured 'Clouds', that new age/ambient anthem that relaunched his career after it was sampled by both To Rococo Rot and Björk. It's a fleeting moment, but it's packed to the brim with the good stuff: humid post-Vangelis pads, synthetic choirs and reflecting pools of reverb. And the atmosphere's pierced by loping rhythms almost immediately; 'Lost' matches its elasticated brass moans with a low-slung beat and then 'The Age of Sampling' appears to hark back to the Fairlight era, conjuring up an industrial soundscape with jerky low-bitrate drum hits, dialog samples and inclement textures that sound like they belong on Black Rain's 'Neuromancer' soundtrack.

The title track is even more surprising, a slippery 120bpm house groover that sounds as if it's been precision engineered for hazy sunrises, with sax wails and vocal pads ducking behind its rubbery beats. If that sounds a bit much, then there's a few quieter spells, like the piano-led 'UMI' and the Shuttle358-inspired closer 'Fifteen', but you can tell that for Masin, "ambient" doesn't mean beatless. The highlight, 'Deception Dance', sounds like classic beardy back-room techno, even - the sort of twitchy biz Carl Craig used to engineer when he was still moonlighting as 69.

items.body:
Bruce remixes Quade's 2025 LP 'The Foel Tower' on a limited cassette for his Poorly Knit label.

"Back in 2023, Bruce was approached by a band of young and ambitious lads, who wanted him to mix their debut album 'Nacre'. Being fans of his music, they hoped to utilise his renowned, club-informed and emotive sound design to add a shade of hypnotism and psychedelia to their singular strand of post-rock. The band of course were Quade, and the union proved to make perfect sense: Bruce excelled in gracefully fulfilling the band's vision, sealing their relationship for projects to come.

A couple years on, both Quade and Bruce had really proved the scope of their abilities: the sophomore album 'The Foel Tower' won the hearts of fans and critics across the board, who celebrated its "gorgeous" and "tender" sound to great acclaim. The world they had built clearly stood defined and dignified, though at the same time, Bruce couldn't help but wonder if there was more to be said. Besides, the sheer abundance of emotion and rich textures therein, suggested a great deal of potential for further exploring. So with the band’s blessing, he embarked on versioning the album.

Bruce was off the leash: total freedom leant him the ability to dub in wild style, weaving and wrestling with drum, bass et al, connecting to the arrangements' true feelings and expanding them to full frame. The "doomer sad boy, ambient-dub, folk, experimental post-rock" of the original, was blown into a whole new, hypnotic realm: through rattling analogue distortion and huge spaced out effects, Bruce's efforts stand as an exploding supernova of dub and noise, refracted through the band's themes of grief, beauty and the great British countryside.

To be released on his label Poorly Knit, this remix album once again proves Bruce's deft of touch and skill in reworking material. Maximising the sonic potential of such a promising and talented band he marks his personal contribution towards what will surely continue to be a fulfilling and illustrious musical journey for Quade."

items.body:
Following frontman Elias Rønnenfelt's indie throwback smash 'Speak Daggers', cult Danish band Iceage continue to shave down post-punk until it looks more like Britpop. RIYL Fontaines DC, Liars or Gilla Band.

It wouldn't be fair to say that Iceage divided its fanbase when they released the sleek 'Seek Shelter' back in 2021. The album was a surprise to their early champions who'd watched them move from noisy hardcore towards a Talking Heads-indebted post-punk sound, but it was also pretty universally acclaimed, its relative polish deemed acceptable because the songs were genuinely pretty catchy. 'For the Love of Grace & the Hereafter' arrives five years later and in the wake of Rønnenfelt's newfound notoriety - both as a solo star and a tabloid staple. So you can almost predict what direction the band have gone in; their sixth album is their most digestible yet, making its predecessor sound almost rough around the edges in comparison.

Rønnenfelt, for his part, actually sounds refreshed, his voice falling between Shane McGowan's and Bobby Gilespie's and for our money handling the pitchy oddball routine a lot more convincingly than Geese's Cameron Winter. But still, it's better suited to angular material like the Byrne-esque 'Match Head Girl' than it is to melodramatic indie-pop gear like 'No Fear' or Strokes-ish material like 'Tender Blades'. The album will probably be huge, it's just chewy like that - they should take Dean Blunt on tour with them.

items.body:
Christopher Tignor’s 'Bleeding Past the Edges' on Western Vinyl.

"Bleeding Past the Edges stands as a deliberate counterpoint to today’s AI-driven music landscape, placing the human hand firmly at the center of creation. Working from a small studio filled with violin, tuning forks, pedals, and custom software, Tignor has developed a performance system that behaves less like a machine and more like a living instrument. Rather than relying on loops or backing tracks, he generates each piece in real time, capturing and reshaping sound as he plays.

Bowed violin lines expand into layered patterns, percussive strikes trigger evolving structures, and even a single tuning fork can unfold into a full harmonic field. The result is an immersive, orchestral sound created live by one performer navigating a tightly interwoven system of gesture, timing, and code. Every element begins as a physical action and remains tethered to it, giving the music a sense of immediacy, risk, and presence that carries throughout the record. Across the album, Tignor moves fluidly between rhythm-forward compositions that treat the instrument as a percussive engine and more melodic works rooted in the violin’s expressive core. Lead single “Weight of Words” highlights this balance, unfolding with a sense of narrative clarity that reflects Tignor’s approach to composition. He often describes these pieces as “short stories,” with melodies acting as the central thread, guiding each work through shifting structures and emotional arcs.

The title Bleeding Past the Edges points to moments when the music pushes beyond its original design, when structure loosens and sound spills outward. Tignor likens the process to “a man on a wire act,” where careful preparation meets the possibility of real-time transformation. Though the systems are rigorously developed, each performance retains an element of unpre- dictability, allowing the music to continually evolve.

Over the course of ten LPs released via Western Vinyl and New Albion, Tignor has earned wide recognition across classical and experimental circles. The Guardian has called him “absurdly talented,” while Bandcamp highlighted his “sheer technical mastery,” and The New York Times has noted his rare ability to seamlessly integrate computers with acoustic instruments in live performance. The Wire has further praised his compositions for their fluid, evolving structures. Beyond his solo work, Tignor has collaborated with artists such as Rachel Grimes, Helios, Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, John Congleton, and This Will Destroy You. His background bridges multiple disciplines, with a PhD in composition from Princeton University, an MS in computer science from NYU Courant Institute, and a BA from Bard College, where he studied with poet John Ashbery.

With Bleeding Past the Edges, Tignor brings these threads together into a work that feels both rigorously constructed and vividly alive, a record that foregrounds performance, physicality, and the enduring expressive power of human-made sound."

Shed plays to varied strengths on a rave-hungry double pack for Dekmantel, exerting signature, swingeing torque on heavy cuts of breakbeat techno-garage, trance and house.

The man-o-many-monikers settles on his OG alias for a haul of tuff meat motors speaking to his decades of skin in the game. He goes deep with the symphonic strings on a bustling breakbeat techno opener ‘Loot 25’, and percolates the drums with rude garage-techno suss in ‘Everybody’, and a simmering 2-step ace ‘Rave Predator’. Electro meets 2-step and lusher choral pads, kinda like Orbital, in ‘Password (Techno Mix)’, while recycling the same elements in full 4/4 flight on its trance mix, and his knack for proper, deep UK hardcore rufige comes into play on a standout ‘Double Scoop’, whereas ‘Taking You Home’ feels like one of his earliest Detroit techno-type winners, and ‘Rave Echoes’ teases that sound out into sublime, aerial tension with a whiff of Carl Craig & Derrick May’s ‘Relics’ about it.

items.body:
London’s Joe Milli makes it two outta two with a 2nd Livity Sound session wriggling in the space between UKF, outernational offbeats and hard groove techno.

The dancer’s joy of pure repetition fuels Milli’s follow-up to the ace ‘Deep Forest’ 12” of 2025. Four-to-the-‘floor kicks knit with potent polyrhythms and Brazilian hoots and hollers in the brisk, sinuous hard groove of ‘Retreat’, and ‘Mantra’ keeps the pace up there with coiled subs and acres of space between the drums for proper loosey goosey movers. On the other hand, ‘Revival’ yokes it back to a heavier, syncopated sort of proto-UKF hoof, adjacent gqom and UK Afro-house flavours, and ‘The less You Know’ also pares it back to slinkiest triplets for clockwork hips.

items.body:
Copenhagen’s meme-able, custom line of genre-blurring songwriters yields Lithuanian talent, Gintè Preisait, fresh from the conservatoire and an LP with Toshimaru Nakamura, on an enchanted, waking dream blend of lower case concrète, trip hop and avant-classical experimentation calling to mind the refined crafts of ML Buch, Ugné Uma, Svitlana Nianio, Smerz, Lucrecia Dalt, Julia Holter or Martyna Basta, thru the reaches of Finland’s Fonal Records.

It was bound to happen at some point, right? We've written more than enough about how Copenhagen's Rhythmic Music Conservatory has become the central node in a scene that's prioritized the permeable membrane between pop, classical training and unhinged technological experimentation - honestly where else are you gonna find Clarissa Connelly, Astrid Sonne, Erika de Casier, ML Buch and Fine? Gintė Preisaitė pushes even further into uncharted waters on her debut album, letting the pop forms evaporate like vapors around her intricately woven experimental collages. We're already off to a good start with 'Vigilance', a lengthy introduction that pays its respects to Preisaitė's past, present and future. The classically trained improviser, producer and composer begins with an ensemble of moaning acoustic instruments that she gradually chips into, tearing through the acoustic sounds with electronic treatments and introducing subtle, grounding field recordings before adding her voice and completely shifting the direction. 

The unwieldy blend of elements prepares us for an arguably bolder experiment, 'Summary Saint Mary', where Preisaitė matches her gamelan-like prepared piano phrases with Björk-ish vocal loops, OPN-inspired electronic touches and wheezing processed acoustic sounds. And it's remarkably well controlled; even in capable hands, it's a tough palette to work with and Preisaitė makes it look almost easy, never stepping too far in any direction or another. Because it's not really a pop record at all, it's an album that's aware of pop, doesn't avoid its charms, but manages to corral its characteristics into the avant garde's misshapen spirit. Even the relatively upbeat, straightforward 'Aéroport', a track that would have sounded stylistically comfortable on Smerz's RMC love-in 'Big city life EDITS', she never goes full James K, letting the melodies curve towards freeform abstraction in the final act before hitting us with three tracks of choppy, half-dissolved prepared piano. It's ambitious stuff, and all the better for it.

items.body:
Avant-pop composer LA Timpa returns to Lolina’s Relaxin Records with a new LP that takes the owner’s rangy license to go dead hypnagogic and heat-sick queasy - FFO Hype Williams, LINTD, Klein, Gray, A.R. Kane.

One down the line from ‘IOX’, the aching abstract keen of ‘Glued to the TV’ connotes a sense of scuzzy stasis in half-lit scenarios that find LA Timpa’s melancholic, strung-out songwriting pushed harder into a sort of bittersweet blooz. Ghostly semblances of song structures remain, but eviscerated to resonant reflections of themselves, like loner laments heard down rusting pipes from the next floor. It’s their most oblique and fascinating turn, arriving 10 years since their debut (‘Animal - EP’, Slow Release) and betraying a robust confidence in their manner of abstract expressionism.

Prizing a droning, sensory obliteration that joins dots between the VU, MBV, A.R. Kane, Hype Williams and Klein, the London-based artist is liberally swaddled in distortion and room-recorded fidelity that only grows thicker, luxuriously lo-fi psychedelic as the album unfolds. The mantric grind and swaying harmonies of ‘Inconsiderate Boyfriend’ set out an aesthetic that he bends to will, variously sinking wholly into dream-pop chamber drone on ‘Toss’, and like a slurred Gray in ‘Carl Mastermind’, but also reserving the right to jam on a classic psych-pop tip in ‘Downtown Spanish Fruit’, and the looped delirium of ‘show me how good you are’. 

His grasp of richly evocative, weathered psych-noise texturing achieves an apex in the 8 mins of pulped spirit to Bond’, and his tilt into A.R. Kane dream-pop listlessness on ‘Msgrievings’, whilst ‘Agenda’ sounds like a communal psych-pop jam enacted by a bin fire, feelings like the mushy dose is waning and the song form is most beautifully struggling to bleed thru.

items.body:
Returning after a 13 year absence, Boards of Canada's vision of hell isn't exactly surprising, swapping out the magic hour guitars of 'The Campfire Headphase' and the tired Carpenter-isms of 'Tomorrow's Harvest' for jagged distortions, dialog snippets and uneasy religious symbolism.

It can't be easy for Mike Sandison and Marcus Eoin; as soon as they cracked the code with 'Music Has the Right to Children' in 1998, their home-brewed signature sound - tape-warped, reverb-soaked monosynths, stuttering dialog samples and thumping MPC-breaks - became a sort of meme, regurgitated by a wave of bedroom musicians so frequently that the original references became fully hollow. Those early records were great because they sounded so unique, marking a landscape littered with post-'Chiastic Slide' crunches and choppy AFX-ian amens with new channels of thought. Just go back to their shadowy 'Twoism', 'Hi Scores', or that Mask 500 cover of 'Midas Touch' -  there was nowt else like it. By the time we got to 'The Campfire Headphase', a comparatively sunny, guitar-led misstep that arrived a few years later and then 2013's 'Tomorrow's Harvest' -  it all felt like diminishing returns.

'Inferno''s mysterious VHS rollout also felt overly familiar - and if you're gonna tease, the payoff best be worth it. Sadly, first single 'Prophecy At 1420 MHz' was damp and old fashioned, lumpen with boxy '80s drums and awkward prog rock synths - the signs didn't look good. Heard as a whole though, 'Inferno' hangs together pretty well. The brothers do a good job of laying out a vision of hell that's intricately connected to their well-worn source material: the lost future that was promised to wide-eyed 1970s kids raised on color TV, welfare and action figures. Back then, religious cults and street cranks were screaming of damnation, convincing weakened minds that judgement was coming while the Vietnam War raged - real hell was on the doorstep all along. And it's hard not to hear Boards' blend of seemingly old-fashioned religious symbolism (the Hare Krishna chants, chopped-up divinity school lectures and guided meditations) as an indirect reference to the wars raging right now. Certainly, it's their darkest album in years; not the aesthetic darkness of 'Tomorrow's Harvest', either. 'Father and Son', with its eerie Abrahamic symbolism, feels like an American Gothic reflection of Leslie Nielsen's comparatively benign narrations on 'Geogaddi', while 'Memory Death' feels like Boards actively sending off their own patented brand of hauntology with the EKG blip to prove it.

Throughout the record, BoC appear to juxtapose a cultural concept of hell with their own aesthetic responses, balancing dystopian robot voices with squelchy acid gurgles on the excellent 'The Word Becomes Flesh' and Bobby Beausoleil-style chiming strings on 'Blood in the Labyrinth'.  'The Process', meanwhile, offers a late-stage vision of aviation hell, a 'Langoliers'-style horror cue that neatly precedes the saccharine vintage BoC hit of 'You Retreat in Time and Space'. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it's these beatless moments that really hold things together - maybe they should have just leaned into it and done a full length of those vignettes. Still, 'Inferno' has its moments.

items.body:
London-based musician Tom Wheatley enlists an ensemble of collaborators - including bagpipe player Harry Górski-Brown and saxophonist Jean-Luc Guionnet - to build a fittingly tense electroacoustic accompaniment to Giulio Bertelli's "techno realist" feature film 'AGON'.

Imagining an Olympic Games in the fictional Italian city of Ludoj, 'AGON' follows three women, each competing in a different event: judo, fencing and rifle shooting. The events were filmed completely on soundstages with no audience, so that each movement could be captured in vivid detail. So reacting to this, Wheatley decided to match a different musician (and instrument) to each athlete: percussionist Seijiro Murayama, who's played in Fushitsusha and K.K. Null‘s noise/rock band A.N.P., was assigned to judo; German cellist Ute Kanngießer to fencing; and horn player Jean-Luc Guionnet to shooting. And to create a sonic backdrop that sat behind the Olympic events, a world at war, Wheatley called up sound artist Grundik Kasyansky and Górski-Brown.

It's a smart way of approaching a film that's so rooted in allegory. The performances are all broadly representative: a 'Fencing Accident' is captured by Kanngießer's strained cello tones and the film's grotesque foley, while Guionnet's slow, measured xenharmonic horn tones shadow athlete Alex Sokolov as she treks through an icy landscape on 'Snow Stalking'. Nothing is obvious or apparent, sounds emerge and vanish and we get to follow their progress as if we're watching the film itself. And if you've seen the film already, don't even begin to think you've heard everything the score has to offer - there's an extra side of bonus tracks.

items.body:
Florida artist Josh Mason (Digitalis, Desire Path + Longform Editions) lands back on Students Of Decay with a new LP partially unearthed from a dormant hard-drive.

"Josh Mason’s new collection, "Wave Salt +7," emerges from an oblique origin. Unearthed from a dormant hard drive, it documents a set of work sessions only partially recoverable, their original continuity and intent fractured by time and technical failure. What remains is a constellation of mercurial gestures that proves, against all odds, to be entirely consonant with Mason’s ongoing musical concerns.

In a sense, the very condition of partiality proves generative, with elision operating on multiple levels - structural, sonic, and archival - shaping both the music itself and the circumstances of its (re)appearance. Phrases surface only to be truncated or displaced, hovering at the edge of resolution, and transitions are implied rather than fully enacted. Absence functions not as a deficit, but as an important compositional resource.

Central to the album’s sound is a distinctive use of vocoding. Deployed not to simulate vocal presence but as a tool for tonal sculpting, it yields a shifting lattice of smeared harmonics, angular melody, and attenuated noise. Sounds are pressed through one another, their edges softened, shifted, or selectively erased, producing surfaces simultaneously articulated and porous. Rather than reconstructing a lost whole, the album posits a mode of listening attuned to gaps, interruptions, and unstable forms. Even so, in keeping with Mason’s broader practice, this music remains grounded in melodic logic and a distinctly human scale, ensuring that its fragmentary structures register not solely as experiments, but as expressions of proximity and feeling."

items.body:
Italian avant chamber quartet Tellkujira turn cues from protests outside the Pompidou Centre, during their IRCAM residency, into a mix of fractious vortices and poetic documentary combining aspects of post-rock and contemporary classical...

“The music of La lucha es un poema colectivo was conceived and composed during a long artistic residency at IRCAM in Paris in November 2023 and will be released by Superpang. ‘In November 2023, we were in residence in Paris when we found ourselves in the midst of protests and strikes by workers at the Centre Georges Pompidou. They were demanding the respect of their rights. Entering that place as outsiders, making art while hundreds of people outside risked losing their jobs, was disorienting.

This is the starting point for the title of this album, evocative yet at the same time tangible. A phrase, as often happens, borrowed from those who had, in turn, borrowed it before us, words that are not and cannot be only ours. Words too heavy to be slaves to context or syntax, yet words that resonate within us, move us, and open rifts in our history as a group. A strange plunge, strange despite the fact that the premises were clear from the start, with well-defined lines of a unified design. And if we ask ourselves, looking around, not so much what but rather with whom we would like to share it, we imagine the music of this album within that groove, in that intangible bond that unites a collective of people who, upon reading this sentence written on a wall, in a street, pause for a moment, slow down, rest their gaze, and know they are still alive.”

Epic 2 hour trip of astral-planing, ambient psychedelia shimmering with displaced traces of pop, slurred acid grooves and ample flange. Definitely one for the road or rail trip this summer, and FFO The KLF, Fennesz, Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, Eno.

items.body:
Jan Jelinek and Alan Abrahams of Portable/Bodycode fame come together on perhaps the most substantial new Jelinek project in years - recalling his own classic Gramm and Farben projects with this low-lit set of simmering, frayed House burners. Really stong!

The two were on each other's radars for years, but didn't come in contact properly until Abrahams brought Jelinek to play at one of his Süd Electronic parties, where they began to mull over the idea of a collaboration. Over the years, they built up a rapport; Abrahams would fire over material that Jelinek would work into the stems, slowly building up the confidence to take more and more risks. He began to fixate on Abrahams voice, ignoring the rest of the instrumentation and threaded it through his usual lattice of concrète sounds in a sort of classic Farben mode.

Farben's a good reference point, particularly for 'Forever', the set's housey-est cut. Jelinek explains in the accompanying press release that the raw vocal had reminded him of "classic house" and that's where we start, with jazzy keys gassing up Abrahams' soulful vox. By the time we hit the halfway point, Jelinek's processes have taken over, with buzzing synths and snowballing percussion that create a dense wall of insectoid noise and interference before the track fades dramatically to silence. It's the most propulsive material Jelinek's been involved with for ages; on '87BPM', he sways Abrahams' wordless groans into a trotting, ping pong shuffle and 'All One' does a thing with tape stop melodies and drunken vocals that sound like an offcut from the CMYK series of EPs.

items.body:
Featuring Matchess and Patrick Shiroishi, 'Rococo ∞ Echomatter' pairs the unstoppable Masami Akita with Chicago-based sound artist and Signal Noise founder Kikù Hibino.

Back in 2024, Hibino invited Merzbow to perform at the Signal Noise showcase at Tokyo's punk venue Bushbash, following it up with 'Sedonis', the noise legend's first release on Signal Noise just a year later. Now the duo cement their friendship with a deafening collaboration, a "cinematic exchange" that centres around Akita's whirring oscillations. Hibino listened in at first just for gaps to splice in his responses, adding vocal contributions from Alexandra Cupsa at first and imagining the edits were something like Godard's 'À bout de souffle' jump cuts. 

Soon his process was bolder, treating Akita's material like concrète sound to be sculpted and moulded. 'saxxxrum' is a particular highlight, lifted by a manic horn improvisation from Shiroshi, but meeting noise with a different kind of noise isn't exactly novel. 'Echomatter' is actually more shocking, when Hibino balances out Akita's drilling, whirring cacophony with surprisingly celestial synths, hitting on a Berlin-school kosmische note almost by accident. And  the lengthy Matchess collaboration 'ƒƒƒ fraa filum flammm' is another chase pick, collaging textured noise in three dimensions and interrupting the anarchy with Whitney Johnson's droll ad libs.

items.body:
For the first time since ’93, Stuart Baker’s prodigious survey of London jazz precedents and curios resurfaces on his Soul Jazz label, packing rare groove heat ranging from Alive!’s Afro-Brazilian bustle to Airot Moreira’s joyous latin jazz and Doug Richardson’s slick salsa. FFO Gilles Peterson, Shabaka Hutchings, Nubya Garcia and Ezra Collective...

“‘London Jazz Classics’ originally came out in 1993 - the first album ever to be released on Soul Jazz Records. The album brought together rare and obscure dance tracks in a unique mix of jazz dance and fusion, funk, Brazilian and Latin grooves.

The album was ironically titled - none of the music was from London, none of the music was traditionally classified as jazz, and all of the tracks were at the time practically unknown to most people. Instead, these were tracks that were filling dancefloors in a nascent jazz dance scene in London being created by a small group of DJs - Paul Murphy, Gilles Peterson, Sylvester, Patrick Forge and a few others. As demand for these rare groove jazz tracks grew, previously unknown records such as Alive!’s ‘Skindo Le Le’, Doug Richardson’s ‘Salsa Mama’, Carlos Franzetti’s ‘Cocoa Funk’ and Emilio Santiago’s ‘Bananeira’ became sort after and even-harder-to-find items with original copies going for 100s of pounds.

These tracks became part of the soundtrack to this jazz dance scene which has now spread across the world. This music paved the way for the arrival of many of the UK’s new wave of current artists such as Shabaka Hutchings, Nubya Garcia and Ezra Collective, who today offer a uniquely London sensibility of fusing jazz with wide-ranging cultural influences - everything from Afrobeat to soul. ‘London Jazz Classics’ was the first album to bring the jazz dance music featured here to a wider audience. More than 30 years since its initial release, Soul Jazz Records release this new 2026 edition, bringing the music to a new generation of listeners once more.

Chicago don Heavee does signature, fast-fwd future funk with ample soul in his 2nd Hyperdub drop.

A Teklife member since the 2010s, who can call DJ Rashad & DJ Spinn mentors, Heavee has pursued his own vein of fluoro-colour machine funk to the hilt with dozens of comp and single shots for footwork’s finest houses. His ‘Mainframe EP’ plays out four flavours for ravers in quicksilver motion, percolating proper gettohouse drums with syrupy acid soul in ‘What U Need’, beside the breathless pressure of a ‘Work it Out’ highlight that goes heavy on the subbass sauce and sublime tension. items.body:
Syrian-Armenian-American singer and producer KÁRYYN returns with second album, PHYSICS UNIVERSAL LOVE LANGUAGE (PULL), via Mute.

"KÁRYYN creates music at the intersection of sound, spirit, and physics – sonic worlds that don’t just describe emotion, they conduct it. PHYSICS UNIVERSAL LOVE LANGUAGE exemplifies this with a title that encapsulates her lifelong endeavour to translate love into systems of energy and truth. At its heart, PULL is about courage: the courage to collapse, to love, to surrender, and to emerge.

Sonically, PULL is crafted from KÁRYYN’s voice, strings, modular synths, and gravitational beats, tuned to 432Hz – a frequency believed to support vibrational healing. Co-produced by KÁRYYN alongside Hudson Mohawke and James Ford, the record was further enriched by Marta Salogni’s sensitive and immersive mix, Jacques Greene’s melodic touch on ‘FWD’, and Joker’s detailed mastering. The result is a meticulously crafted work that is both deeply personal and expansively communal.

PULL is a bold, transcendent journey through KÁRYYN's own human revolution. It is about gravity. About the collapse and coherence that define human experience. It is, in every way, a gravitational pull toward the truth: a sonic architecture of love, rupture, and rebirth."

Sharpie Smile guitarist Cole Berliner brings his "ambient chamber folk" concept to Drag City with 'The Black Door'. FFO Bert Jansch, Marc Ribot and Jim O'Rourke's 'Bad Timing'.

It might be too cloyingly American for some listeners, but 'The Black Door' is undoubtedly well done. Berliner's a skilled player and a provocative arranger, who's knowledgeable enough about American musical history to move his polite parlor music into different chambers. Because although 'A Western Sun' sounds like it's being played in the back room of a saloon in 'McCabe and Mrs. Miller' extended universe, that world melts before our ears on 'Poppies', when Berliner interrupts the sounds with radio interference and washy instrumentation. It's a technique he repeats throughout the record, paying his respects to American folk music's history while simultaneously edging it towards more experimental pastures.

items.body:
Sydney-based drummer Laurence Pike lands on Balmat with a solo fusion of jazz, post-rock and trip-hop that nestles between Burnt Friedman, Makaya McCraven and Barry Adamson.

Remember Pivot? Or Triosk? The Leaf-signed experimental jazz outfit that famously fabricated the ace '1+3+1' LP with Jan Jelinek way back in 2003? Pike's been active on the international scene for what seems like forever - he even joined Liars in 2018. And 'Possible Utpias...' is his follow-up to 2024's ambitious "requiem mass for drums, electronics and choir" 'The Undreamt-of Centre'. Thankfully, this one's a little more approachable than that; there's no quartet to be found, it's just Pike and his gear, imagining what kind of music a jazz musician from an "idealized culture of the future" might make. 

It's a fascinating concept that drives a selection of impeccably played and produced sketches that Pike fleshes out with a little help from his friends: Ben Lerner on alto horn and Novak Manojlovic on keys. But it's Pike's affair and he's most successful when he disregards jazz altogether. On the excellent 'Night Bird', a whirring beat is juxtaposed with Michael Mann-like FM synths and an eerie, wide-open environment and the title track relegates Pike's percussion to the deep background, letting it scrape and scratch beneath dreamy electric piano repetitions.

Japan’s Friday Night Plans & Ena hatch a late night haze of slowcore shoegaze strums and trip hop blooz in dreamy debut fusion for Barcelona’s MOM, and fans of Grouper, Ekin Fil, Eiko Ishibashi.

“Blue Hour is the most recent release from Friday Night Plans, recently signed by Modern Obscure Music. The project marks FNP's shift from their ‘pop’ roots towards a more experimental and ambient sound.

Friday Night Plans is pioneered by singer/songwriter Masumi who has collaborated on this project with acclaimed Japanese producer Ena. Together, they have created a collection of songs that represents the quiet introspection and emotions of the AM hours, using improvisation during the production process to create a cyclical record that is described as ‘dreamlike’.

Masumi attributes the project to a journey consisting of fragments of memory through each song; a reflection of how nostalgia and recollection connects us to emotions.”
